retro.headline: Committee voted to hire Rich Matthew as director of finance and operations, pending contract; requested $300,000 free cash for special ed reserve.
retro.summary: The School Committee publicly interviewed a finance director candidate and voted unanimously to hire him pending contract negotiations. It also approved FY27 line item transfers, surplus literacy materials, a 0.5 OT position change, the paraprofessional contract, and a request for special education reserve funding. Discussion covered MCAS and DIBELS results, Brooks House, and track and field turf costs.

what_happened.line: The School Committee voted unanimously to hire a director of finance and operations, pending contract negotiations, after a public interview.
The Committee voted unanimously to request free cash for the special education reserve fund, if certified at the November town meeting.
The Committee voted unanimously to accept new terms of the paraprofessional contract.
Members voted unanimously to accept FY27 line item transfers and to change a previously voted position to a 0.5 position.
A member said track and field drainage and wall repairs appear to cost about a million dollars before turf; no vote was taken.

why_it_matters: The free cash request rides on the November town meeting warrant article, so residents at that meeting will be asked to certify the money that funds the special education reserve.
The new finance director and the new paraprofessional contract terms shape who prepares the school budget and what a staffing line costs in coming budgets.
Track and field costs have no resolution yet, so a capital request may reach residents later.
watch_next: The November town meeting, where free cash for the special education reserve is to be certified.
The next School Committee meeting, where facilities staff are to present steps and a timeline for the track and field project.

retro.headline: Commission approved several septic and other compliance certificates and two NOIs, and continued most hearings to October 21.
retro.summary: The Conservation Commission heard a planning director presentation on four draft zoning amendments, then worked through a long hearing list. Most hearings were continued to October 21; the Sunny Hill Road driveway, the Goodrich Street irrigation pond and the Pleasant Street septic were approved. The commission also approved eight certificates of compliance and authorized spending on the Hollis Road house.

what_happened.line: The commission approved three notices of intent: a driveway crossing at Sunny Hill Road, an irrigation pond on Goodrich Street, and a septic replacement on Pleasant Street.
Most other hearings were continued to October 21, including 3 Wilderwood Avenue, 37 Fire Road 10, 386 Sunset Lane, 143 Island Road, 404 Page Street, and the Mass Ave sites.
The commission approved certificates of compliance for properties on Sunset Lane, Island Road, Laurel Lane, Beiel Street and White Street, each by 5-0.
For the Hollis Road house, the commission approved a flooring proposal paid from the Hollis Road account and capped paint and supplies spending.
The planning director presented four draft zoning amendments, with comments due at the end of November.

why_it_matters: Approved notices of intent set the conditions for work near wetlands in town, and the continued hearings on Wilderwood, Fire Road and Sunset Lane stay open to public comment on October 21.
The draft zoning amendments on senior housing, inclusionary, cluster and minor site plan rules could change what can be built in town, and residents can still comment before the end of November.
Hollis Road house repairs are drawing on a dedicated commission account, and a plan to put a caretaker on the town payroll would need a town meeting article that residents would vote on.
watch_next: October 21: continued hearings resume, including 3 Wilderwood Avenue, 37 Fire Road 10 and 386 Sunset Lane.
End of November: deadline for comments on the four draft zoning amendments.

retro.headline: Board set Lunenburg Middle High gym as Nov 3 polling place and put several articles on the Nov 17 warrant.
retro.summary: The Select Board granted a common victualler license to Kiku Asian Cuisine, re-voted the polling location after the cafeteria proved too small, and discussed the future of the tri-board and bylaw cleanup for committees. It reviewed the November 17 special town meeting warrant, including several articles and holds for later. The board also discussed municipal building consolidation, a personnel committee liaison, and an early voting location agreement.

what_happened.line: The Select Board voted unanimously to hold the Nov 3 election at the Lunenburg Middle High School gymnasium, after the cafeteria proved too small.

The board voted unanimously to put the omnibus budget amendment, a prior-year bill payment, the special education reserve transfer, zoning corrections and the stormwater fee article on the Nov 17 warrant.
The board held several articles off the warrant for now, including track and field engineering, veterans exemptions, the PEG Access fund, trust funds and classification plan changes.
The board voted unanimously to put a non-binding question on the TC Passios demolition on the warrant.
The board left the tri-board's future open and will seek a joint meeting with the municipal building design committee before special town meeting.

why_it_matters: Residents voting Nov 3 should go to the gym, not the cafeteria, and the Nov 17 special town meeting warrant now lists the articles they will be asked to vote on.
The special education reserve transfer and the budget amendment draw on town money, and the held track and field engineering article may return after the finance committee hearing.
watch_next: Special town meeting on Nov 17, with a possible joint meeting with the municipal building design committee on Monday Nov 2.
The held articles, including track and field engineering, which the board tied to the finance committee hearing and a presentation.

retro.headline: Commission voted unanimously to support the food pantry's variance for modular units, and to seek a joint meeting on the Brooks House.
retro.summary: The Architectural Preservation District Commission welcomed new member Molly, then heard from the Lunenburg Community Food Pantry president about placing temporary modular units at 30 School Street. The chair walked through the commission's concerns with the village center district and the building commissioner's "permanent building" classification. The commission voted by roll call to support the variance with amended wording, and later voted to request a joint meeting with the select board before any Brooks House presentation to town meeting.

what_happened.line: The commission voted unanimously by roll call to support the food pantry's variance for temporary modular units at 30 School Street, with amended wording.
The amended statement says the commission would have recommended the ZBA deny the variance but supports approval given the pantry's work.
The commission voted unanimously to request a joint meeting with the select board before any Brooks House presentation to town meeting.
The chair will send the revised statement to members and check with the ZBA chair whether it goes in writing or by in-person presentation at the ZBA meeting on the 14th.
A possible demolition article for the old town building (TC Pacios) will go on a future agenda, and approval of prior minutes was deferred.

why_it_matters: The commission's statement goes to the ZBA, which decides the pantry's variance, so it bears on whether temporary units can be placed at a village center site.
A joint meeting on the Brooks House comes before any presentation to town meeting, so the commission and select board may align first on a building project residents could be asked to vote on.
watch_next: The ZBA meeting on the 14th, where the commission's statement may be presented in writing or in person.
The next commission meeting, probably early November, set after the chair speaks with the select board chair.

retro.headline: Committee agreed it is too early for a November warrant article and kept shaping a square-footage-and-cost RFP package.
retro.summary: The Municipal Building Design Committee approved prior minutes and agreed it cannot request funding at the November town meeting because no dollar figure exists yet. Most of the meeting was brainstorming what the RFP package should cover: meeting rooms, accessibility, parking, storage, annex options, and the aim of narrowing square footage and cost. The senior-housing grant item was dropped, and the next meeting was set for the 26th.

what_happened.line: The committee agreed it is too early to put a funding article on the November town meeting warrant, because no dollar figure exists yet.
The chair will tell the select board that an article would be premature.
The committee settled on an RFP package aimed at square footage and a cost range, not building design.
The senior-housing grant item was removed from the agenda as outside the committee's charge; broader community-center needs wait until after the fall town meeting.
The chair will ask the town clerk for the monthly meeting calendar and seek a sample architectural RFP; the next meeting was set for the 26th.

why_it_matters: No municipal building funding question will be on the November ballot or town meeting floor, so voters will not be asked to approve a dollar figure until the RFP work produces a cost range.

The RFP is meant to give voters a square-footage and cost range to decide on later, so what it covers (meeting rooms, accessibility, parking, annex options) will shape the size of any future town office request.
watch_next: Next committee meeting on the 26th, on Zoom and in person at the Ritter building.
The sample architectural RFP the chair is to circulate, and the town clerk's meeting calendar.

retro.headline: School Committee unanimously approved a new director of finance and operations title and hired a temporary director.
retro.summary: A short meeting with two items. The committee voted to change the business administrator job description and title to director of finance and operations, adding facilities, technology, transportation, athletics and food service duties. It then approved a retired finance official as temporary director, three days a week, to close out FY26 and build FY27. The superintendent also reported the new athletic director gave 30 days' notice.

what_happened.line: The School Committee voted unanimously, by roll call, to retitle the business administrator job as director of finance and operations.
The new title adds facilities, technology, transportation, athletics and food service duties to the role.
The committee voted unanimously to approve a temporary director of finance and operations, available three days a week, to close out FY26 and build FY27.
The superintendent is to prepare the temporary director's contract; if a permanent director is hired, the temporary director would overlap for cleanup and the FY28 budget build.
The superintendent reported the athletic director resigned on 30 days' notice, and a half-time athletic director position has been posted.

why_it_matters: The person who prepares and presents the school budget is changing, with an interim in place for the FY26 close-out and FY27 work and a permanent hire not yet made, so the FY28 budget build may be done by someone new.

The broader title puts facilities, technology, transportation, athletics and food service under one finance-and-operations role, and the minutes say the duties were widened to match a higher salary, which touches the administration side of the school budget.
watch_next: Next School Committee meeting, Wednesday, October 7, expected to run longer.
The temporary director's contract, which the superintendent is to prepare.

retro.headline: Parks Commission reviewed the beach season and field fees; fee and Wallace Court lighting decisions were put off to the next meeting.
retro.summary: The commission heard facility and recreation updates, a recap of the summer beach season (lifeguard shortage, pass sales shifting toward day passes), and a budget check-in on the parks and revolving accounts. Most of the meeting was a long discussion of raising field usage fees with Lunenburg youth baseball, ending with a request for usage and cost data before any decision. A vote on Wallace Court lighting was deferred until the full commission can attend, and prior minutes were approved with a correction.

what_happened.line: The Parks Commission put off any decision on raising field usage fees until baseball usage data and maintenance and mowing costs are sent in.
A vote on Wallace Court lighting was deferred to the next agenda so the full commission can be present.
The commission heard a beach season recap and a budget check-in; beach revenue rose but did not cover the salary gap, with the revolving account making up the difference.
A youth baseball league representative described the league's field contributions and fees and cautioned against large fee increases.
The commission said it does not sign the community room MOU, which is between the recreation department and the library.

why_it_matters: Field fees for youth leagues were discussed but not set, so any increase would come at a later meeting after usage and cost data are in.
The beach runs on a revolving account that covers what the town's contribution and revenue do not, so a lifeguard shortage or weaker pass sales can leave that account to absorb the gap.
watch_next: The next Parks Commission agenda, which is to carry the field usage fee discussion and a Wallace Court lighting vote once baseball data and cost figures arrive.
The next meeting date, which the chair will set by polling members.

retro.headline: Assessors voted to put two veterans-exemption articles, clauses 22I and 22J, on the November 17 town meeting warrant.
retro.summary: The board approved two sets of executive session minutes, then reviewed classification hearing preparations. The commercial and industrial valuations from Vision are a month late, and the hearing date is tight. It then voted separately to submit two Hero Act warrant articles, one tying veterans exemptions to inflation and one roughly doubling them. Town counsel may still change the wording or require staggering.

what_happened.line: The Board of Assessors voted to place two veterans-exemption articles, clauses 22I and 22J, on the town meeting warrant; the tally was not audible.
Clause 22I ties the veterans exemption increase to inflation (CPI); clause 22J would double the exemptions. The board voted on each separately.
If town counsel says both cannot be adopted in the same year, the board would propose the doubling article (22J) first; the chair will ask counsel.
The board noted the cost of the exemptions falls on the town with no state reimbursement; a member will prepare tax impact figures for the town manager.
The board prefers a Nov 24 classification hearing over Dec 1 and will press Vision for the commercial and industrial data, which is late.

why_it_matters: If town meeting adopts either article, the exemption cost is shifted onto other taxpayers' bills, because the state does not reimburse it.
The late commercial and industrial valuations could squeeze the classification hearing, which sets how the tax burden is split between homes and businesses.
watch_next: Town counsel's answer on whether 22I and 22J can both be adopted in one year, and any change to the wording.
The October 14 agenda, where pending exemption applications were deferred.

retro.headline: Sewer Commission discussed raising the late-payment interest rate and demand fee to match nearby towns; no vote was taken.
retro.summary: The commission approved the prior minutes and heard the first-quarter FY27 demand notice and delinquency report. Most of the meeting was open discussion of raising the late interest rate and the demand fee toward what comparable towns charge. Members leaned toward about 14% interest and a fee between the two figures floated. Nothing was voted; the town manager or staff will ask town counsel about legal limits, and a posted public hearing would be needed. A brief contract update and the meeting calendar followed.

what_happened.line: The Sewer Commission took no vote on raising the late-payment interest rate or the demand fee, and carried the question as a continuing agenda item.
Members reached informal consensus on starting figures of about 14% interest and a demand fee between the two amounts discussed, to be taken to town counsel.
Staff will ask town counsel about legal limits; any change needs a posted public hearing and a place on a future agenda.
Staff said Lunenburg has the lowest late interest rate among the comparable towns on the spreadsheet, and that the demand fee has not changed in about 15 years.
Staff will report at the next meeting on when new bid language goes out for the operations contract, which runs through November.

why_it_matters: Sewer users who pay late could face a higher interest rate and a higher quarterly demand fee, and fee income is meant to support the sewer enterprise fund rather than the general tax levy.
Nothing changes until a public hearing is posted and held, so residents will have a chance to comment before any new rate or fee takes effect.
watch_next: Next meeting October 13 at 6 p.m. (hybrid at the DPW): town counsel's advice on limits, and the contract bid-language timing.
A posted public hearing on any change to the late interest rate or demand fee.

retro.summary: After an executive session on the fire chief, the Select Board voted on the polling location, a police officer appointment, an earth removal renewal, a car dealer license, an open meeting law response, the fire chief contract and an appointment policy. It also reviewed handbook chapters, discussed warrant articles for the special town meeting, and heard committee reports.

what_happened.line: The Select Board voted 4-0 to designate the middle school cafeteria as the polling place, contingent on an accessibility study.
The board ratified the employment agreement for the fire chief, running from the current chief's retirement to mid-2029; the vote was unanimous.
The board accepted the findings in an open meeting law response letter and authorized the chair to sign and submit it, unanimously.
The board ratified a full-time police officer appointment, approved an earth removal renewal, and granted a class 2 auto dealer license, all unanimously.
The board adopted a revised appointment policy as amended, then discussed the special town meeting warrant without settling its articles.

why_it_matters: The polling place decision sets where residents vote, though registrars asked that the general election be held at TC Pacios rather than a school and the designation depends on an accessibility study.

Items discussed for the special town meeting warrant, including school-side funding requests and a possible transfer of free cash to a special education reserve, are ones residents may be asked to vote on, with amounts not yet set.
watch_next: Stormwater and school committee presentations on October 20, and handbook chapters 1-6 returning at the next meeting.
The town manager's walkthrough of the school cafeteria with the superintendent, and the accessibility study the polling place vote depends on.

retro.summary: The board held four public hearings. It approved the 149 Summer Street site plan modification with added conditions and approved both phases of 10 Parmenter Road after rewording several conditions (construction schedule, third-party review deposit, inspection before occupancy, deed language for stormwater maintenance). what_happened.line: The Planning Board approved both phases of 10 Parmenter Road after amending the draft decision's conditions, including stormwater maintenance deed language for all lots.
The board approved the 149 Summer Street site plan modification with conditions added in deliberations.
The 30 School Street food pantry hearing was continued to October 19 at 6:01 p.m., pending the applicant's zoning board variance.
The board voted to waive application fees for 30 School Street, excluding notice and advertising fees, which had already been paid.
Third-party review deposit condition for 10 Parmenter Road: the applicant deposits a fraction of the estimated review cost before a building permit, with supplements as needed.

retro.headline: Commission says school department is illegally withholding scholarship trust records; records request due Sept 26
retro.summary: The Trust Fund Commission (two members present) spent most of the meeting on its ongoing dispute with the school department over scholarship and charitable gift funds, saying the district lacks authority to distribute money without producing the underlying trust declarations and citing a public records request due back September 26. It also discussed advertising and eligibility for the Nathaniel Day Poor Fund and the American Legion Fund, a warrant article for the November special town meeting on the board's authority to act without a full commission, outreach plans, and a standing vacancy for a third commissioner. No substantive votes were taken; the meeting adjourned after a motion.

what_happened.line: The commission says the school department cannot distribute scholarship trust money without producing the underlying trust declarations, and will withhold advertising trust funds until it does.
A public records request to the school department, town manager, select board and treasurer for scholarship fund records was sent September 5, with a response window closing September 26.
The commission finalized a warrant article for the November special town meeting on its authority to act without a full three-member board.
No votes were taken; the commission also postponed finalizing declarations for three other funds and delayed advertising the Nathaniel Day Poor Fund pending legal review.

why_it_matters: Scholarship money held in school-related trust funds may stay undistributed to students until the records dispute with the district is resolved.
Residents seeking help from the Nathaniel Day Poor Fund or American Legion Fund will see delayed advertising and applications while legal review and the school records dispute continue.
A warrant article at the November special town meeting would change how the commission -- currently missing a third member -- is allowed to act.
watch_next: Public records response from the school department due back September 26
November special town meeting warrant article on the commission's authority without a full board

retro.headline: FinCom will likely fund an outside review of the school department's FY26 budget overruns from its reserve
retro.summary: The Finance Committee got a preliminary, informational run-through of draft special town meeting warrant articles (zoning, stormwater fees, a veterans' exemption increase, PAC salaries, a $195,830 track/turf engineering request, and a special education reserve fund transfer) ahead of an October 8 discussion and October 22 public hearing for a November 17 special town meeting. The bulk of the meeting concerned a planned outside financial operations review of the school department's FY26 budget variance, to be funded from the Finance Committee's reserve account once a firm and scope are chosen; members also discussed possible tri-board meetings, a DLS workshop on financial policy, and committee reports on the municipal building project, the library, and the school finance director search.

what_happened.line: The Finance Committee expects to fund an outside review of the school department's FY26 budget variance from its own reserve account.

Draft special town meeting articles got a first look -- stormwater fees, a veterans' exemption increase, PAC salaries, a track/turf field engineering request, and a special education reserve transfer.
Those articles move to an in-depth discussion October 8 and a public hearing October 22, ahead of a November 17 special town meeting.
A workshop on net school spending was tabled because the presenter could not attend.
Whether to hold joint tri-board meetings, on topics including an athletics budget and ambulance billing write-offs, was left to the three board chairs to work out.

why_it_matters: The planned review would look at why the school department's FY26 spending diverged from its budget, a question tied to special education placement costs.
The special education reserve transfer, the track/turf field funding, and a possible veterans' exemption increase would all go to voters at the November 17 special town meeting.
A new stormwater fee structure, discussed at this meeting, could show up as a separate charge on future bills depending on how the article is written.
watch_next: October 8 in-depth discussion of the special town meeting warrant articles
November 17 special town meeting

retro.headline: Cemetery Commission approved August minutes, reviewed the back-lot expansion bid timing, and moved its maintenance rules toward a separate policy.
retro.summary: The commission approved the prior minutes, heard a resident urge green burial and volunteer landscaping, and was told the North Cemetery back-lot expansion spec is ready to go to procurement, with work hoped to be substantially done by December. Members compared proposed rules and regulations against Chapter 310 and agreed in general to keep maintenance policy separate from the public-facing rules, with Copilot-assisted merging to follow. The next meeting was moved from October 29 to Wednesday October 28.

what_happened.line: The commission moved to keep its maintenance policy separate from the public-facing Chapter 310 rules, with a member to merge the versions using Copilot and bring them back.
The commission was told the North Cemetery back-lot expansion spec is ready for procurement, with work hoped to be substantially done by December.
An updated cost estimate for the expansion came back unchanged, and the chair expects capital funds plus commission-allocated funds to cover it.
The commission will explore natural burial over time, including talking to a neighboring DPW director, with no near-term action because conventional inventory is ample.
The next meeting was moved to Wednesday the 28th instead of Thursday the 29th, pending availability.

why_it_matters: The back-lot expansion adds burial space and is paid from capital funds and commission-allocated funds, so the bid result decides whether those funds cover it.
The rules and fee schedule residents are charged under are being rewritten, and the commission treated the fee schedule as done and to be placed in the rules.
Residents asking for green burial or native landscaping heard that natural burial will be explored over time, with no near-term action, so near-term changes should not be expected.
watch_next: The next meeting, moved to Wednesday October 28, pending availability, where the merged rules and maintenance policy are due back.
The procurement bid for the back-lot expansion, which could come in lower if let late in the season.

retro.headline: Chair refused a commissioner's PFAS/manganese cost-saving proposal presentation, deferring it to next meeting.
retro.summary: The Water District Commissioners discussed IT/cybersecurity costs, adopted an informal policy requiring commissioners to give advance notice before adding substantive items to the agenda, and voted to put water-quality (PFAS/manganese) data on the district website. The bulk of the meeting was a heated dispute over whether a commissioner could present, that day, a proposal to avoid a roughly $40 million treatment plant by blending well water; the chair deferred it to the next meeting pending input from DEP, and the district also reported progress on the Metal Lane/Rolling Acres water main project.

what_happened.line: The chair declined to let a commissioner present his plan to blend well water instead of building a new treatment plant, deferring it to the next meeting pending state DEP input.
Commissioners voted to post the district's manganese and PFAS testing data and charts on its website, updated at least quarterly.
The board set an informal rule that a commissioner must request an agenda item through the clerk-treasurer in advance rather than raise it the day of a meeting.
A commissioner argued the standard PFAS/manganese treatment approach carries a large capital cost plus an ongoing annual operating cost, and said well-blending could avoid both if DEP approves it.

why_it_matters: Which treatment path the district picks for PFAS and manganese -- a new plant or well-blending -- will set the size of a capital project that ratepayers eventually finance through water rates.
Public posting of the water-quality data lets residents check manganese and PFAS levels themselves rather than take the board's word for it.
The new advance-notice rule for agenda items changes how a commissioner or resident gets a substantive proposal in front of the board on a given meeting date.
watch_next: Next Water District meeting: the well-blending proposal, circulated by email beforehand, comes back for discussion
A DEP meeting expected around October on whether well-blending is a viable alternative to the treatment plant

retro.headline: Assessors tabled a plan to expand veterans' property-tax exemptions until the chair weighs in
retro.summary: The Board of Assessors, missing its chair for the whole meeting, covered office relocation, an unfilled data-collector position, ongoing neighborhood/site-index revaluation work with a consultant, and preparations for a tax classification hearing tentatively set for November 17. It also discussed two warrant articles that would expand and CPI-index veterans' property tax exemptions but voted to table that discussion until the chair could take part, and closed by scheduling a special meeting for September 30 and entering executive session.

what_happened.line: The board tabled draft warrant articles expanding veterans' property-tax exemptions until the chair, absent all meeting, can take part.
A special meeting was set for September 30 specifically to take up and possibly vote on that exemption language with the chair present.
The assessor was asked to prepare individual, outlier-level home value changes rather than only group averages, ahead of a tax classification hearing.
The board is trying to set a tax classification hearing for November 17, coordinated with the Select Board, with backup dates in reserve.
Approval of executive-session minutes was pushed to September 30 because they had not yet been printed.

why_it_matters: A change to veterans' exemptions affects who qualifies for tax relief and, since the town covers the cost above the state reimbursement cap, how much is absorbed by other taxpayers.

The tax classification hearing sets how the overall tax burden splits between residential and commercial/industrial property, and the individual (not just averaged) value data will show whether some homeowners see increases well above the town-wide figure.
Residents following the veterans exemption proposal or worried about a sharp assessment increase on their own home will not see a decision until the chair returns.
watch_next: September 30 special meeting: vote on veterans exemption clause language with the chair present
Tentative November 17 tax classification hearing, paired with a Select Board meeting

retro.headline: Task force voted to draft a support letter for a 604B watershed grant and set dates for FinCom, Select Board and a public session.
retro.summary: The task force compared funding stormwater work through a utility versus the operating budget, discussing staffing (a junior engineer or project manager, partly shared with DPW), outsourcing versus hiring, and the effect on resident bills. It scheduled presentations (Select Board Oct 20, FinCom Oct 22) and a public info session Nov 9 at the library's Wallace room. It reviewed draft fee and abatement slides and the 604B grant, then voted on a support letter and minutes.

what_happened.line: The task force voted 4-0 by roll call to have the consultant draft a letter of support for a 604B watershed grant application, to be signed electronically.
Dates were set: Select Board presentation Oct 20, FinCom Oct 22, and a public info session Monday Nov 9 at 7 p.m. in the library's Wallace room.
The task force compared funding stormwater through a utility versus the operating budget; the two differ in administrative overhead, not in the cost of the work.
State and charitable properties will be left out of fee billing, and the abatement review interval will change from 10 years toward 3.
A virtual slide review was set for Thursday Oct 15, with slides going to the boards by the end of Friday Oct 16 or over the weekend.

why_it_matters: Whether stormwater is paid through a separate utility fee or through the tax levy decides how the cost lands on a household's bill, and residents will hear both options before any vote on one.

The task force has not yet chosen between the two, and the fee design (exempt properties, abatement interval) is still being revised, so the terms residents are shown in November may differ from the current drafts.
watch_next: Select Board presentation Oct 20 and FinCom Oct 22, with a public info session Nov 9 at 7 p.m. at the library.
The Oct 15 slide review and the revised fee and abatement slides due to the boards by Oct 16.

retro.summary: The Municipal Building Design Committee approved prior minutes, then discussed a rough square-footage estimate for consolidated town offices, built from an AI-assisted sizing exercise. Members debated Ritter/annex options, storage, the cable-access group's (PAC) space needs, and the case for one building. They agreed to work on a scope of work (not called an RFP) at the next meeting and ended with a roll-call adjournment.

what_happened.line: The committee agreed its next meeting will start drafting a scope of work for an architect, deliberately not called an RFP, to take to the select board.
Members discussed a rough space estimate for consolidated town offices, produced by an AI-assisted sizing exercise; no vote was taken on it.
Options for the Ritter building and an annex, plus parking, accessibility and storage, were debated without resolution.
The chair is to invite the cable-access group's representative, and a member is to estimate how much records storage is held now.
The next meeting was set for October 5 because the 19th conflicts with the planning board; the chair's residency is an agenda item.

why_it_matters: A scope of work is the step before hiring an architect, and members expected a concept-level study to cost tens of thousands of dollars, so how it is funded could decide whether residents are asked to vote at town meeting.
The size estimate is a rough, AI-assisted range, so any cost figure built on it will also be a wide range until an architect studies the buildings.
watch_next: The draft scope of work for an architect, which the committee planned to begin at its October 5 meeting, and whether it goes to the select board.
The agenda item on the chair's residency and ability to chair at that meeting.
